INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Eightieth Report of the Committee on the Code of Civil Procedure(Amendment) Bill, 2000*.
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred ** the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on December 22, 2000 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.0       The Committee considered the Bill in five sittings held on 11 June, 11 & 12 July, 17 October and 2 November, 2001.
3.1       The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs in its sitting held on 11 June 2001.
3.2       In its sittings held on 11 & 12 July, 2001, the Committee heard  Chairman and Members of Bar Council of India, President of Supreme Court  Bar Association and Former Judge of  High Court of Delhi , respectively,  on the various provisions of the Bill.
3.3       In its sitting held on 17 October 2001, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
3.4       The Committee considered the draft Report in its sitting held on 2 November 2001 and adopted the same.  It also decided that the evidence tendered before the Committee may be laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament.
4.0       In course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill and took note of the recommendations of various Law Commissions,  replies to queries raised by the Members on the Bill in the meetings, submitted by the Legislative Department and suggestions/observations tendered by  the witnesses.
5.                  For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT
 
            The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000 (See Annexure-I) seeks to amend Code of the Civil Procedure, 1908 (hereinafter referred as Code) and the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.
2.0       The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 which came into force w.e.f. 1 January, 1909 contains Laws relating to the procedure in suit and civil proceeding in India except in the case of State of Jammu and Kashmir, Nagaland, Tribal areas of Assam and certain other areas.12.1.0    The code is mainly divided into two parts :-
(i)         Sections – (158 Sections divided under 21 Parts)
(ii)
                Orders & Rules -  (51 Orders under the First Schedule of the Code)
 
2.1.1    Sections contain main principles while the detailed procedures with regard to matters dealt with by the Sections are specified in Orders and Rules.
2.2.0    The Code of Civil Procedure, being in List-III-Concurrent List2 in Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, is amenable    to amendments by the Acts of both Union and State Legislatures3.  Furthermore, the High Courts are also empowered to amend, by rule, the Code. It may be highlighted that the Union/State Legislatures can amend both Sections and Orders of the Code whereas the High Courts can bring in amendments to the Orders only.4
2.2.1    The Code has been amended innumerable times by the Acts of Union/State Legislatures. So far the Code has been amended sixty-six times approximately by Parliament.
2.3.0    The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 (See Annexure-II) was enacted by Parliament and assented to by the President on 30 December, 19995
 but was not brought into force due to strong opposition to the same from various quarters.
2.3.1    The aforesaid Act was enacted on the basis of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997  which was introduced as an official Bill in the Rajya Sabha on 14 August, 1997.
2.3.2    The Bill was introduced to bring in comprehensive changes in the Code to expedite the disposal of civil suits and proceedings so as to ensure that justice was not delayed.
2.3.3    The CPC (Amendment) Bill, 1997 was referred to this Committee on 19 August, 1997 for examination and report. The Committee, in turn, had presented its Forty-ninth Report on the Bill to Parliament on 17 December, 1998.
2.3.4    The Committee had considered the thirty six clauses contained in the Bill and recommended changes in six clauses (clause Nos.1,9, 26, 29, 33 and 34) and recommended no changes in twenty eight clauses (clause Nos. 2 to 8, 10 to 25, 27, 28, 32 and 35) and recommended for dropping of two clauses (clause Nos. 31 and 36).
2.3.5    Almost all the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Report referred above were accepted by the Government and was, accordingly, reflected in the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999.  In effect, the CPC (Amendment) Act had thirty four Sections after dropping two clauses from the CPC (Amendment) Bill, 1997.
2.4.0    The amendments to the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 have been necessitated due to numerous representations from Members of Parliament, members of the Bar, Bar Councils, individuals and other quarters like Law Commission of India.
2.4.1    The Law Commission of India under the Chairmanship of  Shri  Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy presented its One Hundred Sixty-third Report  on 13 November 1998 wherein it had suggested in great detail a re-look  at some of  the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill 1997 (Clause Nos 2,7, 10 to 20, 23, 24, 26 to 28 and 30 to 32).  The Ministry has admitted that the recommendations of Law Commission on the aforesaid Bill could not be taken  into account while enacting the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.
 2.4.2   The Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000 contains seventeen clauses out of which there are four altogether new clauses in addition to commencement clauses i.e. clause 1, clause 16 which makes consequential amendments and clause 17 which is repeal and saving clause.  The remaining ten clauses of the said Bill intents to either substitute or amend the provisions of the 1999 Act.
2.4.3
        The proposals contained  in the Bill, 2000 can  be classified broadly into two groups:-
(a)    Amendment to the Code of Civil Procedure ,  1908
(b)   Amendment to the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999

(A) NEW AMENDMENTS IN THE CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE, 1908
2.5.0    Amongst the seven proposed new amendments in the Code as contained in the Bill, three are based on the recommendations contained in the Law Commission’s Reports which are as below:-
(i)
                  Clause 2 based on One Hundred Forty-fourth Report;
(ii)                Clause 3 based on Fifty-fourth Report; and
(iii)               Clause 14 based on One Hundred Thirty-ninth Report.
 
The remaining Clauses are 1, 13, 16 and 17 of the Bill.
2.5.1    In addition to the above seven new amendments, one is partially new as it seeks to amend both the Code and the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 i.e. clause 12 of the Bill:-
Sub clause (a) of the clause amends rule 2 of Order XVIII of the Code, and the sub-clause  (b) of the clause of the Bill amends Section 27 of the 1999 Act i.e. rule 4 of Order XVIII of the Code.
The clause has been analysed in great detail in para No. 2.22.0 of the Report.
 2.6.0.  Clause 2 intends to incorporate a clarification under Section 39  - “Transfer of decree” - of the Code which says that the court cannot execute a decree against a person or property outside the local limits of its jurisdiction. 
2.7.0    Clause 3 proposes to insert a new sub-section to Section 64 - “ Private alienation  of Property after attachment to be void” - of the Code.  This would, in effect, resolve the conflict of decisions with a view to clarifying that a transfer or delivery of property, etc. in pursuance of any contract entered into and registered before the attachment shall not become void.

2.8.0    Clause 13 amends sub-rule (1) of rule 1 of Order XX to fix time limit for pronouncement of a judgement as it is felt that reserved judgements should be delivered within a reasonable time.  It is therefore proposed that the courts shall make an endeavour to pronounce a judgement within thirty days from the date on which the hearing of the case is concluded.  Where it is not practicable to do so on the ground of exceptional and extraordinary circumstances of the case, the court shall pronounce the judgement ordinarily within sixty days from the date on which hearing was concluded.
2.9.0    Clause 14 has two parts – The first part of the clause inserts an explanation to sub-rule  (5)  of rule 32 of Order XXI with a view to removing doubts as to whether  the expression  The act required to be done  covers only mandatory injunction or prohibitory injunction or both.
2.9.1    It is pertinent to explain that rule 32  of  Order XXI  provides  for punishment  for disobedience to an injunction  issued by the Court.  Sub-rule  (5) of rule 32 provides that where a decree for specific performance of a contract or for an injunction has not been obeyed, the Court may direct that the act required to be done may be done  by the  decree  holder or some other person appointed by the Court at the cost of judgment debtor.
2.9.2    Now the explanation  to be inserted in the aforesaid rule would   imply that the act required to be done would cover both prohibitory as well as mandatory injunction.
2.9.3    The second part of  Clause 14 seeks to amend rule 92 of Order XXI  to bring congruity between  article 127 of Limitation Act, 1963 and  sub-rule (2) of rule 92 of Order XXI. 
2.9.4    It may be mentioned that initially an application   to set aside   an execution sale  (which is required   to be accompanied by deposit of requisite amount in the Court, to the decree holder by the judgment debtor) was thirty days.  The period of thirty days is insufficient to enable the judgment debtor to arrange for requisite fund having regard to the fact that Banks usually take more than thirty days to sanction loans and advances. Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963 was amended in 1976 and time for making application stood increased to sixty days from thirty days.
2.9.5    The Law Commission in its One Hundred Thirty-ninth Report (1991) [Chapter II Para 3.2)] has pointed out that while preparing the Bill for amendment of Limitation Act, 1963, amendment to corresponding provision in the CPC i.e. sub-rule (2) of rule 92 of Order XXI escaped the notice of draftsmen inadvertently.  The net position is that while time for making application is sixty days whereas the time for making deposit (supposed to accompany the application) remains unaltered as thirty days. Now the amendment in the CPC through the said clause would increase the period for making deposit to sixty days so as to establish congruity between Limitation Act and the CPC.
B. AMENDMENT TO THE CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE (AMENDMENT)   ACT, 1999
2.10.0  Letters Patent Appeal (LPA):  Clause 4 of the Bill amends Section 100 A of Code as substituted by Section 10 of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 which is relating to Letters Patent Appeal (LPA).
2.10.1  Certain High Courts including chartered High Courts have been empowered to entertain appeals against decree or order of its single Judge to Division Bench under Letters Patent Appeal (LPA).  Under the scheme of LPA, appeal can be preferred against the decree or order of a single Judge in two cases:
(i)                  original jurisdiction (Section 96 of the Code); and
(ii)                Extra-ordinary jurisdiction (Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution).
2.10.2  To check appeal against the decree pronounced in the exercise of original power of the High Court as permissible under Section 96 of the Code, the CPC wasamended way back in February 1976 by inserting a new Section (100A) under the heading of “Appeals from appellate decree”.
2.10.3  By the Act of 46 of 1999, Section 100A was substituted again in order to prohibit second appeal from its original decree along with extra-ordinary decree to Division Bench.
2.10.4  The above provision in the Act is same as clause 10 of the CPC (Amendment) Bill, 1997 and introduced in order to implement the recommendations of Justice V.S. Malimath Committee.  The Committee in its Forty-ninth Report had also adopted the clause.
2.10.5  By virtue of 1999 Amendment Act, the Letters Patent Appeal against the judgement and decree of a single Judge made in the appeal preferred under Section 96 of the Code as well as the Letters Patent Appeal preferred against the judgement and order of a single judge in an application made under Articles  226 and 227 of the Constitution was sought to be done away with altogether.
2.10.6  The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report (vide para 2.6.1) has observed that there is strong and uniform opposition from the members of the Bench and the Bar that abolition of Letters Patent Appeal against the judgement of a single judge made on an application under Article 226 would add enormously to the burden of the Supreme Court because the only remedy would then be available to approach the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.
2.10.7  The Law Commission has pointed out that appeal lie straight against the original decree of Single Judge of Allahabad High Court to the Supreme Court under Article 226 since 19626 and has burdened the Supreme Court.
2.10.8  As regards Article 227 of the Constitution, the practice is not uniform.  In some States appeal under Article 227 is treated at par with an application under Article 226, thereby has the scope of second appeal.
2.10.9  The Law Commission in the said Report (para 2.8.3) had recommended strongly against the abolition of LPA against the judgement pronounced by single judge on an application made under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution.
2.10.10  As regards the abolition of LPA against the judgement of a single Judge made in an appeal against decree (under Section 96 of the Code) which was taken away in 1976, the Commission observed that it should be exercised in the following restricted manner:
(i)                  appeal should be against final  decree/judgement not interlocutory/interim order; and
(ii)                the appeal in the suit should involve substantial question of law on the lines of Section 100 of the Code.
 
2.10.11   The Government has introduced the CPC (Amendment) Bill, 2000 to restore Section 100 A to its pre-1999 position not pre-1976 position.
2.10.12     The Bar Council of India (BCI) has suggested to restore LPA to its pre-1976 position (decree pronounced in exercise of both original as well as extra-ordinary jurisdiction)
2.10.13     The Legislative Department has commented that it would be a retrogative step and thus is not acceptable.
2.10.14      The Committee agrees with the comments of the Legislative Department.
2.10.15     Appeal and Revision: Clause 5 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 11 of the  Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 so as to bring some desirable  changes in Section 102 of the Code.
2.10.16    Section 102 of the Code, before 1999 amendments, prohibits second appeal in certain cases which satisfies the following two conditions:-
(i)
                  the suit is of a nature cognizable by a court of small cause; and
(ii)                the value of the subject matter of the suit does not exceed three thousand rupees.
 
The 1999 Act eliminated the requirement at (i) supra and increased the valuation of subject matter of the suit mentioned at (ii) supra from rupees three thousand to twenty-five thousand  (in view of depreciation in the value of money).  The net position of Section 102 after   1999 amendment  is  that no second appeal in all cases where the value  of subject matter of the suit does not exceed rupees twenty five thousand. 
2.10.17     The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third  Report  has suggested that restriction as to the nature and character of the suit be dropped as it felt that the Section 102 might entail grave injustice to suit for mere permanent injunctions which are valued at low figures unrelated to the subject-matter of the suit.
2.10.18    Thus clause 5 of the Bill intends to substitute Section 102 of the Code  in a way to confine its application to money suit only, the reason being that money suits are comparatively simple suits and Order XXXVII of the Code provides its summary procedure.
2.11     There was no opposition from any quarter to the aforesaid provision of the Bill.
2.12.0  Issue and Service of Summons :        Clause 6 of the Bill seeks to amend Section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 which is related to the provision relating to issue and service of summons laid down inorder V of the Code.  The Clause has two parts and amend clause 15(i) and  (ii) which substitute rules 1 and 9 of Order V, respectively.
2.12.1  Rule 1 of Order V of the Code as stood amended by 1999 Amendment Act empowers  the Court to issue to the defendant  summons to appear and answer the claim on a day to be specified therein, after the institutions of suit.  The following are the main features of the said rule:-
(a)
    The date of appearance of defendant to answer the claim is within thirty  days from the day of the institution of suit;
(b)   Both the appearance and filing of written statement by the defendant are on the same day; and
(c)    In case of failure on the part of defendant to file written statement on the date specified, he shall be allowed by the court to file the same on later day which shall not be beyond thirty days from the date of service of summons on the defendant.
 
The net position is that the date fixed for appearance shall never be beyond thirty days from the institution of suit and the date for filing written defence can never be beyond thirty days from the date of service of summons.
2.13.    The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report has observed that it is necessary to take into account the practical  problem and the realities  of the situation  while  fixing mandatory time limits.  Some of the suits are complicated in nature which call for good amount of preparation by the defendant before filing his defence.  Further, where Government is a defendant, it is not as prompt as a private party in filing the written statement due to the requirement of coordination and internal correspondence  between one Department and the other.  Members of the Bar, who participated  in the conference arranged by Law Commission on the issue, opposed any sort of time limits whereas the members  of the Bench supported the time limits.  However, the members of the Bench felt that the time
limit set by the amendment was unrealistic and might result in failure of justice in some cases.  However, there was consensus that the time limit for thirty days from the date of institution of suit  to be substituted by sixty days from the institution of suit.  In case of failure to file written statement  within thirty days from the date of summons on defendant, the period may be extended to ninety days from the date on which the period of 60 days expires, which has also been recommended by Law Commission.
2.14     Now clause 6 (i) intends to make a provision that the defendant would be required to file written statement in his defence within  thirty days from the date of service of summons  but this period could be extended upto ninety days from the date  summons by the court for reasons to be recorded.
2.15     Here the Law Commission’s recommendation has not been accepted in toto by the Government.  Law Commission recommended to increase the time limit from appearance of defendant from thirty days to sixty days from the date of institution of suit, whereas period of thirty days provided by 1999 Act remains unaltered in the present Bill.  Further-more, the maximum period for submitting written statement recommended by  the Law Commission was 150 days from the date of institution of suit whereas the Bill makes provision  of 90 days from the date of summons.
2.16     There is no opposition to reasonableness of time limit envisaged by the Bill by any of the witnesses and thus appears to appropriate.
2.17.0  Service of Summons :Clause 6 (ii) substitutes the scheme for service of summons envisaged in Section 15 (ii) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 which, is turn,  had amended  rule 9 of Order V.
2.17.1  The Code as stood amended by the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999  envisages the following scheme to serve summons on the defendant:
(a)
    The Court  shall hand over the summons to the plaintiff or his agent, who shall arrange  to serve it  within  two days  from the delivery of summons in the manner provided in (b) below.
(b)   The plaintiff or his agent has to serve the summons on the defendant by
 
(i)                  registered post acknowledgement due; or
(ii)                speed post; or
(iii)               approved courier service; or
(iv)              fax message; or
(v)                Electronic mail service; or
(vi)              other means prescribed by the High Court by rules.
 
The actual mode to be adopted out of (i) to (vi) above, has to be specified by the court. [Vide sub-rule (1) of Rule 9)]
(c)    In addition, the court may also direct service of summon through the proper officer of the court (process server ) (vide rule 9A of order V).
Thus sub-rule (1) of Rule 9 of Order V places the duty of serving summons upon the plaintiff within two days.
2.17.2  The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report has pointed out that supplementary means of serving summons specified in sub-rule (1) of rule of 9 of Order V was treated as welcome step but there was uniform opposition both from the members of the Bar and the Bench to the proposal for serving summon by the plaintiff or his agent on defendant.  It was submitted that summons should be sent in any of the modes specified in sub-rule (1) of rule  of 9, by the court itself, though at the expense of the plaintiff since the present scheme may give room to mischief and fraud.
2.17.3  The Law Commission therein had suggested to make it mandatory or obligatory on the court to service summons through normal mode of delivery of summons i.e. process server and registered post acknowledgement due, in addition to mordern means of transmission at the expense of plaintiff.  Further, the service of summons through plaintiff may be in addition to above method.
2.17.4  The Bill as envisaged under clause 6(ii) contains the following features:
(i)   summons shall be delivered by the process server or such other means approved by the registry of court, itself at the expense of plaintiff.  In addition, summons can also given to the plaintiff for service on defendant
(ii)  no time limit for servicing summon by the court/plaintiff is prescribed (in 1999 Act the period was 2 days for plaintiff).
(iii) panel of courier agencies can be prepared by High Courts or the District Judge
(in 1999 Act it was High Court only).
2.17.5  The Bar Council of India has no objection to the modern means of transmission of summons.  But the President of Supreme Court Bar Association had expressed apprehension about the reliability of fax message and was against privatisation of judicial service by sending summons through courier who are private agencies and may lead to corruption.  He suggested that mode of transmission of summons should be conjuctive not disjunctive.  There must be at least two/three modes of sending summons. If one fails the other would succeed. 
2.17.6  The Committee was of the view that the system of sending summons through process server in lower courts particularly Munsiff Court has been unsatisfactory and felt the need for introduction modern means of transmission for sending summons.  It also  felt that the there should be at least two additional fast means of sending summons to ensure its service on defendant.
2.17.7  As regards courier agencies, the Committee wanted to know how the private parties could be prevented from doing any mischief with the service of summons. The Secretary, Legislative Department  had informed the Committee that the courier agencies were accountable to the court; if they serve wrong document or give wrong statement with regard to failure to deliver the summons, they would be punishable under the Indian Penal Code.
2.17.8  The Department has further informed the Committee that in the State of Tamil Nadu plaintiff can serve summons on defendant, by a way of State amendment to Section 19 A of Order V. The Department do not find merit in the suggestion for introduction of conjunctive mode of serving summons.
2.18.0  Amendment of Pleading:  Clause 7 of the Bill, 2000 seeks to amend Section 16(iii) of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 in order to restore rules 17 & 18 of Order VI in a new form.
2.18.1  Rules 17 & 18 of Order VI stood omitted with the enactment of the CPC (Amendment) Act, 1999 to get expeditious trial of cases.
2.18.2  The Law Commission in its One Hundred Sixty-third Report has recommended to restrict the amendment to plaint to the direction of court to the effect that the amendment is necessitated (i) by change in law subsequent to the framing of the issues (ii) on account of any fact coming to the knowledge of applicant after framing of the issue which could not have been discovered by him with due diligence before framing the issue, once the trial commences.  It has been pointed out that it has the support of members of the Bench.
2.18.3  The provision contained in clause 7 of the Bill intends to implement the above recommendation in toto. TATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            This Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as the Code contains the law relating to the procedure in suits and civil proceedings.  The Code has been amended from time to time by various Acts of Central and State Legislatures.  Recently, the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 was enacted by Parliament with a view to cutting short the delays at various levels.  After its enactment, a large number of representations were received both for and against its enforecement.  The Law Commission of India in its 163rd Report also dealt with the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997 which was enacted later on as the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999.
 
            2. Before action could be initiated for enforcement of the said Act, the Bar Council of India and certain local Bar Associations asked the Government to relook into certain provisions which could cause hardship to the litigants.  Accordingly, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 and other proposals to reduce delay in the disposal of civil cases were discussed with legal luminaries.  The Government has further considered the matter in all its aspects after consulting the Bar Council of India and others concerned and based on the outcome of the deliberations, it is now proposed to further amend the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, consistent with the demands of fair play and justice.
           
            3. The proposed amendments inter alia seek to provide, that ––
(a)         plaintiff shall produce documents and pay requisite fee for service of summons on the defendants within seven days from the date of order by the Court for issue of summons;
(b)         the summons would be served on the defendant by the Court either by its process servers or through private courier agencies approved by the Court.  In addition to the service of summons by the Court, the plaintiff may also serve summons on the defendant;
(c)          a defendant is to file written statement within thirty days from the date of service of summons but such date can be extended up to ninety days by the Court for reasons to be recorded in writing;
(d)         the documents may be produced by the plaintiff or by the defendant, as the case may be, with the leave of the Court at the time of the hearing of the suit where such documents could not be filed by the plaintiff along with the plaint or by the defendant with this written statement.  Rule 14 of Order VII of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, (hereinafter referred to as the “Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act,”) and rule 1A of Order VIII after the amendments made in the year 1999 do not provide an opportunity to the plaintiff or the defendant, as the case may be, to produce documents at the hearing of the suit;
(e)          shall produce documents and pay requisite fee for service of summons on the defendants within seven days from the date of order by the Court for issue of summons;
(f)under rule 5 of Order XIV of the Code, amendment of issues or framing of additional issues may be allowed.  This rule was omitted by clause (ii) of section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act,  1999;
(g)         in place of insertion of sub-rule (2) 1 of XXXIX, a new rule 2B be added which would provide that the stipulation of furnishing security would apply under rule 1 as well as under rule 2 of Order XXXIX.  By section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999, a new sub-rule (2) was inserted in rule 1 of Order XXXIX so as to provide that a person seeking injunction will be required to furnish security by the Court.  This section is proposed to be omitted.
(h)         time-limit  for oral arguments by the parties may be fixed and with the leave of the Court, the parties may be required to submit written arguments before concluding the oral arguments in a case by insertion of a suitable provision in Order XVIII of the Code;
(i)the examination-in-chief of a witness shall be recorded on affidavit.  The cross-examination of a witness in the High Courts having original jurisdiction shall be recorded ordinarily by the Commissioner and in Courts subordinate to the High Court, such evidence shall be recorded either by the Court or by the Commissioner appointed by it.  The Commissioner shall also have the power to record the demeanor of a witness and any objection made in regard to such matter shall be decided by the Court at the time of arguments of the case.  A Commissioner is required to submit his report within six months from the date of issue of the commission.  Rule 4 of Order XVIII as amended in the year 1999 which provided for recording of evidence (cross-examination and re-examination) of the
witnesses by the Commissioners in all cases is proposed to be substituted in this regard.
(j)the judgments are to be pronounced within definite time-frame after a case has been heard.  The general rule proposed is that a judgment is to be pronounced at once and where it is not practicable to do so, the Court shall make an endeavour to pronounce judgment within thirty days from the date on which hearing of the case was concluded.  Where it is not practicable for the Court to pronounce judgment within thirty days because of exceptional and extraordinary circumstances of the case, the Court shall fix a day for  the pronouncement of judgment which shall not ordinarily be beyond sixty days from the date on which the case was heard;
(k)         appeals to division Bench of the High Courts in writs under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution shall be restored, Section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 abolished appeals against judgments of a single Judge of the High Court in all cases;
(l)no second appeal shall lie in money suits where the value of the subject matter in the suit does not exceed rupees twenty-five thousand.  Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 abolished second appeal in all cases where value of the subject-matter in the suit did not exceed rupees twenty-five thousand;
(m)       section 39, section 64 and rules 32 and 92 of Order XXI of the Code, shall be amended on the basis of the 54th , 139th and 144th Reports of the Law Commission of India.  These amendments are clarificatory in nature.

Shri D. V. Subba Rao Chairman, Bar Council of India The Bar has no reservation to the resolution of disputes through the system of Lok Adalats. Wherever there is a clause for arbitration or conciliation or mediation, the law says that you refer the disputes to an arbitrator.  A court may not be in a position to say whether it
can be settled.  Again, arbitration, conciliation and mediation require trained personnel, people who have the capacity to bring the parties together, discuss with them and then bring about a settlement between them.
The Code of Civil Procedure,  1908 prior to its amendment in 1940 contained section 89 regarding the provisions relating to reference to arbitration by the courts.  On enactment of the Arbitration Act, 1940 the said section 89 was omitted.  However, by the Code of
Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1999 section 89 has been reintroduced with a view to empowering the courts to refer cases to arbitration, conciliation etc.  Where the parties to the suit have no objection to such reference.  This provision was introduced with a view to
implementing the Malimath Committee recommendation relating to compulsory conciliation and also to take out certain matters from the docket of the courts where the parties are agreeable to alternate dispute resolution mechanism.
     There is no compulsion requiring any dispute or pending cases to be referred to Lok Adalats for arbitration or conciliation.  At present, the institution of alternate dispute resolution mechanism does not exist on a permanent basis. With the enactment of section 89, it
would be possible to create parallel system of alternate dispute resolution at Taluka level, Tehsil level, District level and State level parallel to the system of courts. Such bodies may be established as permanent bodies either by the Bar or with the assistance of Chambers
of Commerce etc.  It may be provided that the filing of records shall be before courts so that such records may be preserved and copies of records could be provided to the functionaries of the alternate dispute resolution mechanism.
